item.dc:creator: Simon Sharwood
item.content:encoded: Anthropic has started extending access to its bug-finding Mythos model by allowing Cisco and IBM to make it part of their security products. Cisco announced its integration today at an event in Melbourne, Australia, where it revealed that the red teaming tools in its AI Defense suite, which looks for weaknesses and inappropriate activity in AI models, agents, and applications they power, will be able to call Mythos to test customers’ setups. “At a very high level, AI Defense has the ability to look at models and break them,” said Jeff Schultz, Cisco’s senior vice president for portfolio strategy and marketing. He said the tool is now “super-charged by Mythos” and will identify more danger that AI Defense will then address. AI Defense already uses AI-powered red teaming to find flaws. Mythos will become another option. Cisco will make it available under users’ existing licenses, without additional cost. Natalie Mead, Anthropic’s head of applied AI for the Asia-Pacific, said the company has a long queue of buyers who want to use Mythos, and working with Cisco will make it easier to satisfy that demand. Anthropic initially made Mythos available under "Project Glasswing," a program that gave vetted organizations access to the model to test their codebases, but has since expanded access through other controlled programs, an arrangement that makes considerable sense because in the wrong hands Mythos could help attackers exploit software flaws. The Cisco deal exposes the functionality of Mythos to end-users, without letting them use the model itself. The Register asked Mead if Anthropic has similar deals with other third parties and she demurred. That may be because a few hours after Cisco told us about its use of Mythos, IBM announced that it will also integrate Anthropic’s model into a product – namely its Concert tool, which uses AI to scan applications for risks and weaknesses. IBM says it will use Mythos “to uncover weaknesses traditional scanners miss, determine which pose real risk and generate fixes for developer approval.” We have asked Anthropic if these integrations represent a decision to open Mythos to more users in more ways. We will update this story if we receive a substantial response. Also on Monday, Anthropic introduced version 5.2 of Mythos and Fable, which the company says generate outputs up to 30 percent faster than version 5.1 yet cost less: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Users can choose to run both models in “fast mode,” which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times, and doubles prices to $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens. Anthropic says it “ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes.” After those tests, the company concluded “high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. “Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.” The latter is a telling admission, given Anthropic believes Chinese AI labs use distillation to effectively clone its models without doing expensive training work. ®

item.title: France blames Iran for supermarket hack meltdowns
item.description: France has turned up the heat on Iran over destructive cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers at more than 700 grocery stores in October, spoiling food and sparking fires. The country vowed to take action using “all available means of response.” The supermarket attacks , which affected Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour, and Intermarché groups, started at least 15 fires and caused food losses in the tens of millions of euros, according to a Monday report by France’s Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre (C4). The C4 includes the National Cybersecurity Agency of France, the Directorate General for External Security, the Directorate General for Internal Security, the Directorate General for Armament, and the Cyber Defence Command. “This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory,” France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement . All signs point to CyberAv3ngers Both the report and the statement attributed the refrigeration controller hacks to the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) Shahid Kaveh cyber unit. The Shahid Kaveh unit, which French national security officials say is led by Reza Salarvand and Mahdi Lashgarian, is better known by its hacktivist personas, including CyberAv3ngers . This is the same crew suspected of involvement in the July attacks that targeted more than 100 internet-exposed water systems in America. While the US government hasn’t attributed the intrusions to any country or group, private-sector security analysts blamed Iran , and specifically CyberAv3ngers . The IRGC-affiliated hacking crew has been breaking into industrial controllers for years , and in 2023, American national security and law enforcement agencies attributed a series of cyberattacks against "multiple" US water facilities to CyberAv3ngers. “The Iranian cyber threat against French interests is not new,” according to the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “Iran has already carried out several destabilizing acts against us, notably targeting the weekly magazine Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024.” Since at least June 2024, the Shahid Kaveh unit has had the ability to scan, access, and control industrial control equipment from Schneider Electric, Siemens, and Rockwell, the French government said in its report. The country vowed to take action using “all available means of response.” The supermarket attacks , which affected Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour, and Intermarché groups, started at least 15 fires and caused food losses in the tens of millions of euros, according to a Monday report by France’s Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre (C4). The C4 includes the National Cybersecurity Agency of France, the Directorate General for External Security, the Directorate General for Internal Security, the Directorate General for Armament, and the Cyber Defence Command. “This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory,” France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement . All signs point to CyberAv3ngers Both the report and the statement attributed the refrigeration controller hacks to the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) Shahid Kaveh cyber unit. The Shahid Kaveh unit, which French national security officials say is led by Reza Salarvand and Mahdi Lashgarian, is better known by its hacktivist personas, including CyberAv3ngers . This is the same crew suspected of involvement in the July attacks that targeted more than 100 internet-exposed water systems in America. While the US government hasn’t attributed the intrusions to any country or group, private-sector security analysts blamed Iran , and specifically CyberAv3ngers . The IRGC-affiliated hacking crew has been breaking into industrial controllers for years , and in 2023, American national security and law enforcement agencies attributed a series of cyberattacks against "multiple" US water facilities to CyberAv3ngers. “The Iranian cyber threat against French interests is not new,” according to the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “Iran has already carried out several destabilizing acts against us, notably targeting the weekly magazine Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024.” Since at least June 2024, the Shahid Kaveh unit has had the ability to scan, access, and control industrial control equipment from Schneider Electric, Siemens, and Rockwell, the French government said in its report. It pins the refrigeration controller hacks on this particular Iranian crew for a couple of reasons. Making the case for attribution First: the infrastructure used to carry out the October supermarket attacks was also used during this timeframe to conduct reconnaissance on Schneider Electric equipment, zeroing in on small- and medium-sized energy and water production units. “The techniques used during these actions are known to have been used by the Shahid Kaveh unit since at least April 2026,” the report says. It also notes that investigators found “traces of Farsi use” in the attack infrastructure. Plus, Iranian media outlet CyberbanNews, which is reportedly linked to the Shahid Kaveh unit, publicized the incidents that occurred late on October 11 and into October 12 extremely quickly: “as early as October 13.” In early November, similar cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers were reported across Europe , with grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden reporting widespread food losses after miscreants spiked temperatures to as high as 122°F (50°C). Last week, the US federal government urged owners and operators to take security measures to prevent these types of attacks from spreading to America. France fights back The French government, for its part, said that it would “use all available means of response, including within the European Union and alongside its European and international partners, to anticipate, prevent, deter and respond to destabilizing and destructive actions targeting it in cyberspace.” This includes proposing additional EU sanctions against Iranian entities and individuals involved. France also vowed to express “its strongest condemnation of these cyberattacks” to the Iranian ambassador. However, the country didn’t rule out responding with more than just harsh words: “France reserves the right to take any additional measures, public and non-public, deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to these cyberattacks.” ®

item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 9, 1967: NASA launches the Saturn V moon rocket for the first time on Apollo 4, but no astronauts were aboard
item.description: null On Nov. 9, 1967, NASA launched the powerful new Saturn V rocket on its maiden voyage. The Saturn V moon rocket was 363 feet tall. That's taller than the Statue of Liberty! It was the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built at the time (though SpaceX's Starship megarocket has since surpassed it). NASA needed such a powerful rocket to launch astronauts to the moon. However, the first Saturn V launch didn't carry astronauts, because it was only a test flight. During the launch, the rocket created a loud shockwave that surprised nearby observers. The ground shook so hard that it rattled buildings miles away, and all the shaking caused a huge shower of dust and debris NASA's new launch center, the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The mission lasted 8 hours 36 minutes. The rocket carried an uncrewed command module that splashed down in the Pacific Ocean. NASA's first-ever Saturn V rocket launches on its maiden flight from Cape Canaveral, Florida on the uncrewed Apollo 4 test flight on Nov. 9, 1967. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered The launch of Apollo 4 in November 1967 was a turning point for NASA on its path to landing astronauts on the moon. The space agency had bet the moon on its new Saturn V booster, a three-stage heavy-lift rocket designed to fly astronauts in a capsule (as well as their lander) to the moon and back. But the rocket had never been fully tested until the Apollo 4 launch. NASA also needed a new launch site for its Apollo missions. So the agency built Launch Complex 39 at what is now called the Kennedy Space Center, a Florida spaceport that has become the home port for orbital human spaceflight in the United States. But in 1967, no rockets had ever flown from the site. Yet, everything went according to plan. Amazing Apollo 4: NASA's 1st Saturn V Moon Rocket Test Flight in Photos “It was really an expert launching all the way through from lifting off exactly on time to performance of every single stage,” rocket pioneer Wernher von Braun , director of NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, said at the time . The launch came as NASA was on its heels. Just months earlier, on Jan. 27, 1967, the space agency suffered a fatal tragedy when Apollo 1 astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee died on the launch pad after a fire broke out inside their Apollo command module during a ground test. A view of the Apollo 4 launch after stage separation looking back down at Earth from the Saturn V rocket. NASA/Interm Archives/Getty The uncrewed Apollo 4 command module splashes down under parachutes after a smooth test flight. NASA/Interm Archives/Getty “The maiden voyage of the Saturn V dramatically increased the confidence of people across the nation in the management of the largest research and development undertaking in which the western world has ever engaged,” George Mueller, NASA's then-Associate Administrator for Manned Space Flight, said at the time . Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube . item.title: Jupiter and Mars are set for a breathtaking close approach later this week: Here's how to see it
item.description: null Jupiter and Mars will shine side by side in a spectacular close approach in the heart of the constellation Leo on Nov. 15. Here's what you need to know. Mars and Jupiter reach their closest apparent separation in Earth's sky at 9:04 p.m. EST on Nov. 15 (0204 GMT on Nov. 16), according to astronomy website In-The-Sky . The planets will be below the horizon for U.S. stargazers at the moment of their closest approach, but observers can catch the pair rising above the eastern horizon around midnight local time, just a few hours later. Remember: You can discover the exact timings for the rising and setting of the planets above your local horizon using Time and Date's night sky tracker . Jupiter will be the brightest of the pair, when it rises a little over 1 degree from the red light of Mars — roughly the width of your little finger held at arm's length against the night sky. The bright star Regulus will glow close at hand, forming the dot of the backward question mark formation of stars that represents the head of the great Lion in the constellation Leo. Celestron StarSense Explorer LT114AZ (Image credit: Celestron) The Celestron StarSense Explorer LT114AZ is a great way to get a closer look at Jupiter, Mars and Saturn. Its 4.5-inch aperture and a high 1000mm focal length delivers good magnification out of the box, plus it's integrated with the StarSense smartphone app, which makes finding those planets so much easier. Check out our full review for more. Mars and Jupiter will be close enough to share the field of view of a pair of 10x50 binoculars and will also make for a spectacular sight through the eyepiece of a telescope when viewed separately as they rise away from the horizon. The gas giant's iconic Great Red Spot will rotate into view in the predawn hours of Nov. 16, and will be visible through a backyard telescope with an aperture of just 4 inches . Using a light green color filter will help increase the visibility of the vast storm, while an orange filter will help bring out detail in the gas giant's sweeping cloud belts. The two planets will appear to gradually drift apart over the coming weeks and won't appear as close again for another 2.5 years in July 2029 , when the two planets appear close together in the constellation Virgo . Be sure to check out our guide to photographing the night sky , along with our picks of the best cameras and lenses for astrophotography if you're interested in following the dance of the planets for yourself. Editor's Note: If you would like to share your astrophotography with Space.com's readers, then please send your photo(s), comments, and your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.

item.title: Manchester’s soulless content machine football clubs sum up post-imperial Britain | Barney Ronay
item.description: United and City dominate the news cycle with stories so strange and vast they threaten to consume the rest of the league In Manchester this weekend it was possible to bookend your Thursday‑to‑Sunday entertainment with two cultural events. First up, a debut screening of the re‑released and uncensored Ken Russell film The Devils at Trafford Odeon. And three days later, three miles down the road, Manchester United versus Aston Villa at Old Trafford. As expected, one of these events provided a visceral cinematic experience, a deeply disturbing two-hour public meditation on the meaning of faith, blood, fear, power, ritual and the fetishising of objects, climaxing in an orgiastic crowd scene of depraved but undeniably erotic abandon, all acted out on a set in a state of glorious and performative ruin. And the other one was a film with Oliver Reed in it. Continue reading...

item.title: Chioma Ude Celebrates Women in African Cinema at AFRIFF 15 Dinner | See Photos
item.description: For AFRIFF’s 15th anniversary, Chioma Ude made room for a different kind of celebration: an intimate dinner dedicated to the women shaping African cinema. The gathering brought together female filmmakers, producers and directors for an evening of fashion, good food and conversations about the industry they are helping to shape, with plenty of opportunities to catch up and connect outside the usual festival setting. As founder and executive director of the Africa International Film Festival, Chioma established AFRIFF in 2010 to showcase African talent and create more opportunities for filmmakers to reach wider audiences. Fifteen years on, the festival has become an important platform for African cinema, making the dinner a fitting occasion to celebrate some of the women contributing to the industry. The evening also came with a specially curated dining experience by Chef Tolu Eros whose multi-course menu brought West African flavours into a fine-dining setting. Alongside the conversations and fashion, the dinner offered guests a chance to enjoy good food and celebrate the women whose work continues to shape African storytelling. See more photos below The post Chioma Ude Celebrates Women in African Cinema at AFRIFF 15 Dinner | See Photos appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Are the James Webb Space Telescope's mysterious Little Red Dots actually tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang era?
item.description: null Ever since NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) started observing the early universe, it has been providing almost as many surprises as it has answers. One such surprise are the so-called Little Red Dots, cosmic objects that seemingly disappear completely before the universe is two billion years old. New research suggests that Little Red Dots may actually be connected primordial black holes , tiny black holes born not from dying stars but rather from fluctuations in the density of matter just after the Big Bang, in the earliest moments of cosmic history. Should they exist, primordial black holes would predate stars, galactic dust particles, and elements heavier than hydrogen and helium. Now, researchers have used JWST data to test whether one particular Little Red Dot, known as blackAbell 2744-QSO1 (QSO1), could host a primordial black hole. "A black hole is an object born from the gravitational death of a star. Primordial black holes are a very different story," study team member Valerio De Luca, of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at Johns Hopkins University (JHU) in Maryland, said in a statement . "They come from the physics of the early universe that predates the first stars, when the universe was expanding exponentially in time and space. So the mechanisms for creating primordial black holes are different," De Luca added. Little Red Dots could be the smoking gun of primordial black holes Though scientists have theorized about the existence of primordial black holes since they were first proposed by Stephen Hawking in the 1970s, no hard evidence has presented itself. One of the issues scientists have puzzled over is how to tell the difference between a primordial black hole and a "traditional" or astrophysical black hole formed from the supernova death and collapse of a massive star. "Little Red Dots could surround astrophysical black holes, and most probably many of them do, but they could also be primordial black holes, if primordial black holes exist," De Luca said. "So the question becomes, Which ones are primordial and how can we tell?" De Luca and colleagues turned their attention to QS01, located around 13.1 billion light-years from Earth, which is seen as it was just 700 million years after the Big Bang. What makes this Little Red Dot stand out is the fact that it is almost entirely composed of hydrogen and helium. Because these were the universe's first elements, it could be more unspoiled and primordial than other Little Red Dots. The team modeled how a Little Red Dot like QS01 could form from a primordial black hole. That was necessary because the circumstances under which this could happen would have to be very specific. "There are constraints on primordial black holes from cosmological observations," said team member Loris Del Grosso, also of JHU's Department of Physics and Astronomy. item.content:encoded: null Ever since NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) started observing the early universe, it has been providing almost as many surprises as it has answers. One such surprise are the so-called Little Red Dots, cosmic objects that seemingly disappear completely before the universe is two billion years old. New research suggests that Little Red Dots may actually be connected primordial black holes , tiny black holes born not from dying stars but rather from fluctuations in the density of matter just after the Big Bang, in the earliest moments of cosmic history. Should they exist, primordial black holes would predate stars, galactic dust particles, and elements heavier than hydrogen and helium. Now, researchers have used JWST data to test whether one particular Little Red Dot, known as blackAbell 2744-QSO1 (QSO1), could host a primordial black hole. "A black hole is an object born from the gravitational death of a star. Primordial black holes are a very different story," study team member Valerio De Luca, of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at Johns Hopkins University (JHU) in Maryland, said in a statement . "They come from the physics of the early universe that predates the first stars, when the universe was expanding exponentially in time and space. So the mechanisms for creating primordial black holes are different," De Luca added. Little Red Dots could be the smoking gun of primordial black holes Though scientists have theorized about the existence of primordial black holes since they were first proposed by Stephen Hawking in the 1970s, no hard evidence has presented itself. One of the issues scientists have puzzled over is how to tell the difference between a primordial black hole and a "traditional" or astrophysical black hole formed from the supernova death and collapse of a massive star. "Little Red Dots could surround astrophysical black holes, and most probably many of them do, but they could also be primordial black holes, if primordial black holes exist," De Luca said. "So the question becomes, Which ones are primordial and how can we tell?" De Luca and colleagues turned their attention to QS01, located around 13.1 billion light-years from Earth, which is seen as it was just 700 million years after the Big Bang. What makes this Little Red Dot stand out is the fact that it is almost entirely composed of hydrogen and helium. Because these were the universe's first elements, it could be more unspoiled and primordial than other Little Red Dots. The team modeled how a Little Red Dot like QS01 could form from a primordial black hole. That was necessary because the circumstances under which this could happen would have to be very specific. "There are constraints on primordial black holes from cosmological observations," said team member Loris Del Grosso, also of JHU's Department of Physics and Astronomy. "There can only be so many primordial black holes in the universe, for example, and there cannot be too many of them in a given cluster." An image from NIRCam (the Near Infrared Camera) on NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope shows Abell 2744-QSO1. (Image credit: NASA) Considering three possible scenarios, the team found that the most likely situation is a smaller primordial black hole consuming surrounding gas and energy until it grew to be the size of QSO1. "The door was open on this theory — that Little Red Dots could be primordial black holes," Del Grosso said. "We've now cracked it open a little farther by showing some scenarios are more likely than others." An illustration of primordial black holes. (Image credit: University of Massachusetts Amherst) Del Grosso and crew now intend to look at the other 100 or so Little Red Dots seen by the JWST to determine how many of them could have started life as primordial black holes. Then scientists may finally have the evidence to say these long-theorized ancient black holes actually existed. "We don't have a clear understanding of what happens in the early universe right after the Big Bang," De Luca concluded. "If primordial black holes do exist, then something had to happen to make them in the first place, which would be a groundbreaking discovery in physics." The team's findings were published in June in the journal Physical Review Letters.

item.title: Jensen Huang’s image has been shattered. Could he be pushed out at Nvidia?
item.description: Huang built Nvidia as a family business but after the co-founder had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, its board faces a difficult decision For more than 30 years, Jensen Huang has been the seemingly unshakable public face of Nvidia. He co-founded the company as a young engineer in 1993 and oversaw its growth into a multitrillion dollar chipmaker and bellwether of the AI industry at large. He’s also made it a family business. His children, Madison and Spencer, have taken leadership roles at the firm. While not a company executive, his wife, Lori Mills Huang, leads the family foundation which, as of 2024, controls over 60m Nvidia shares. Continue reading...

item.title: 5 Trending Nollywood Movies to Add to Your YouTube Watchlist This Week

Secrets have a way of coming out, family ties can get complicated, and love doesn’t always go according to plan. These are just some of the stories unfolding in this week’s Nollywood releases on YouTube. From psychological drama and riverine mysteries to corporate battles and family betrayals, here are five films bringing different stories to the screen. 7 Years Silence (Bolaji Ogunmola TV) What happens when a web of long-kept secrets finally unravels after nearly a decade? 7 Years Silence follows a devoted wife who, after seven years of marriage and a painful struggle to conceive, discovers her seemingly perfect husband has been living a complete double life. As hidden motives and suppressed truths explode into the open, every character is forced to face the shattering fallout of a marriage built on an illusion. This gripping emotional thriller features standout performances by BamBam ( Bamike Olawunmi – Adenibuyan ), Deyemi Okanlawon , and Teniola Aladese . The River Remembers (Omoni Oboli TV) Love and dark ancestral secrets collide in this haunting riverine drama. Newly engaged Morayo and Akindele travel to his hometown to celebrate their future, but beside a forbidden river, Morayo’s recurring nightmares begin to unearth a devastating truth. As painful revelations draw an unyielding line between their families, the couple is forced to choose between their dream together or losing each other to a past they never chose. Produced by Nollywood powerhouse Omoni Oboli, the movie stars Taye Arimoro , Teniola Aladese , Kunle Omisore , Najite Dede , Olami Samuel , Bridget John , Oyetola Elemosho , Tolu Otebiyi , Paul Word , Taiwo Familoni . Caught in the Cycle (Biodun Stephen TV) Tackling heavy themes of trauma, broken trust, and survival, Caught in the Cycle delivers an intense psychological ride. The narrative centers on a gifted teenage girl whose life takes a terrifying turn after she is taken in by a wealthy couple promising her a brighter future. Instead of sanctuary, she finds herself trapped in a living nightmare of abuse, manipulation, and betrayal—ultimately leading to a shocking crime that forces her to fight with everything she has for her freedom and the truth. Directed by Olubunmi Akingbola and produced by Biodun Stephen , the film relies on raw, high-stakes performances from an impressive cast starring Stan Nze , Angel Unigwe , and Leolidas Ewane . item.title: Attackers backdoor trusted AWS integrations to steal secrets
item.description: Unknown attackers used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access customer AWS environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets. Qubole is a cloud data processing platform that uses cross-account IAM roles to manage compute and access storage in customers' AWS environments without requiring customers to provide long-lived AWS access keys. The supply-chain attack abused this third-party, cross-account trust relationship. Google’s cloud-security shop Wiz declined to tell us how many organizations were affected, but called it a “broad, opportunistic supply chain campaign” that hit “multiple” customer environments. “Because many organizations left trust policies active even after deprecating the platform, the attacker was able to successfully assume integration roles, enumerate cloud resources, harvest secrets, and siphon data,” the researchers told The Register in an emailed response to questions. Qubole did not respond to The Register 's inquiries. Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders after AI data security company Sentra flagged suspicious activity, traced the malicious activity back to October 14, when credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account were used to call the sts:AssumeRole API to obtain temporary credentials for customer-managed integration roles. The calls originated from Qubole AWS account 805246085872 , and used IAM user ID AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS , Wiz analysts Zack Morrow, Sean Johnstone, and Benjamin Read said in a Monday blog about the supply chain attack. “Across the affected environments, Wiz CIRT has not observed this IAM user in any activity other than that associated with this threat actor,” the trio wrote. This activity continued on October 15, and on October 18, the digital intruders began using a second IAM user from the same account. Once inside customers’ environments, the crooks began probing a ton of AWS services and stealing credentials, keys, and other secrets stored across Lambda, Secrets Manager, and SSM Parameter Store. The miscreants also used TruffleHog to test AWS credentials belonging to victim organizations, discover their Microsoft Entra ID secrets, and request OAuth tokens using Okta client credentials also uncovered while snooping around the AWS environments. Abusing the integration roles also allowed the criminals to steal data from customers’ S3 storage, although it seems they were largely opportunistic attackers, in some cases downloading entire buckets, as opposed to state-sponsored spies looking for specific data. The threat hunters haven’t attributed the supply chain attack to any particular group, and say they don’t have any insight into how the miscreants are using the stolen data. While investigating this incident, Wiz spotted a separate campaign between October 8 and October 11 that also used customer-owned AWS access keys for Qubole integrations. item.dc:creator: Jessica Lyons
item.content:encoded: Unknown attackers used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access customer AWS environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets. Qubole is a cloud data processing platform that uses cross-account IAM roles to manage compute and access storage in customers' AWS environments without requiring customers to provide long-lived AWS access keys. The supply-chain attack abused this third-party, cross-account trust relationship. Google’s cloud-security shop Wiz declined to tell us how many organizations were affected, but called it a “broad, opportunistic supply chain campaign” that hit “multiple” customer environments. “Because many organizations left trust policies active even after deprecating the platform, the attacker was able to successfully assume integration roles, enumerate cloud resources, harvest secrets, and siphon data,” the researchers told The Register in an emailed response to questions. Qubole did not respond to The Register 's inquiries. Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders after AI data security company Sentra flagged suspicious activity, traced the malicious activity back to October 14, when credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account were used to call the sts:AssumeRole API to obtain temporary credentials for customer-managed integration roles. The calls originated from Qubole AWS account 805246085872 , and used IAM user ID AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS , Wiz analysts Zack Morrow, Sean Johnstone, and Benjamin Read said in a Monday blog about the supply chain attack. “Across the affected environments, Wiz CIRT has not observed this IAM user in any activity other than that associated with this threat actor,” the trio wrote. This activity continued on October 15, and on October 18, the digital intruders began using a second IAM user from the same account. Once inside customers’ environments, the crooks began probing a ton of AWS services and stealing credentials, keys, and other secrets stored across Lambda, Secrets Manager, and SSM Parameter Store. The miscreants also used TruffleHog to test AWS credentials belonging to victim organizations, discover their Microsoft Entra ID secrets, and request OAuth tokens using Okta client credentials also uncovered while snooping around the AWS environments. Abusing the integration roles also allowed the criminals to steal data from customers’ S3 storage, although it seems they were largely opportunistic attackers, in some cases downloading entire buckets, as opposed to state-sponsored spies looking for specific data. The threat hunters haven’t attributed the supply chain attack to any particular group, and say they don’t have any insight into how the miscreants are using the stolen data. While investigating this incident, Wiz spotted a separate campaign between October 8 and October 11 that also used customer-owned AWS access keys for Qubole integrations. While a “small number” of these also resulted in the intruders compromising victim organizations’ AWS environments, Wiz said it can’t definitively connect the two sets of malicious activity. Organizations that have integrated with Qubole should rotate credentials - although rotating a credential does not end temporary sessions that were already issued. Customers should also review CloudTrail from October 1 onward, looking for AssumeRole events where userIdentity.accountId matches Qubole's AWS account ID, 805246085872, particularly those originating from non-AWS IP addresses. “For every role session you find, review all subsequent activity from that session, especially Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda and S3,” the researchers wrote. “If the threat actor assumed an integration role, rotate every secret, parameter and Lambda environment variable the role could read, and revoke active sessions for the role.” “AWS services were not compromised by this issue and operated as designed," an AWS spokesperson wrote to use after we first published this article. "The activity describes how threat actors used credentials associated with a third-party provider to access some AWS customers’ accounts by assuming IAM roles those customers had configured to trust that provider. As always, we recommend all customers follow security, identity, and compliance best practices, including regularly reviewing cross-account IAM roles, removing access for integrations no longer in use, granting least-privilege permissions, and adding conditions such as source IP restrictions to role trust policies. AWS customers who suspect or become aware of unauthorized activity in their accounts should follow guidance for remediating potentially compromised credentials or contact AWS Support with any questions or concerns about the security of their account.” ® Updated on November 10 with statement from AWS.

item.title: NYT bestseller ‘Robopocalypse’ is getting a TV series with Oscar winners Ron Howard and Akiva Goldsman at the helm
item.description: null They say all good things come to those who wait… and WAIT. Well, the wait for "Robopocalypse" fans might finally be over, as Oscar winners Ron Howard and Akiva Goldsman have announced they're working on a TV adaptation. It does seem like an eternity since news first broke that Portland-based New York Times bestselling author Daniel H. Wilson’s "Robopocalypse" (Doubleday, 2011) was bought by Steven Spielberg’s DreamWorks SKG for a sci-fi spectacle, with Drew Goddard ("The Martian") brought in to pen the screenplay. That was back in 2009, and since then the story of a rogue AI named Archos and a hearty band of indigenous people in America’s heartland battling to save humanity from extinction has been placed on Hollywood’s back burner. After numerous stalled starts and director Michael Bay getting involved in 2018, "Robopocalypse" was quietly powered down due to script issues, filmmaker scheduling conflicts, and the enormous budget required. But now we have been blessed with the news , first broken by The Hollywood Reporter, that Ron Howard ("Apollo 13," "The Da Vinci Code") and Akiva Goldsman ("A Beautiful Mind," "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds") have taken up the mantle of this chilling sci-fi project to develop as a new TV series. And what timing, just as AI fever has gripped the planet with paranoia centered around our eventual robot overlords. "'Robopocalypse' has all the scale and suspense of a major action story, but what drew me to it are the thought-provoking themes and humanity at its center," Ron Howard shared in a statement. The cover of 2011's smash sci-fi hit Robopocalypse by Daniel H. Wilson Vintage The cover of the 2014 sequel Robogenesis by Daniel H. Wilson Vintage "Daniel created a future that feels both startling and increasingly plausible, with characters who must figure out what connects us when the technology we rely on turns against us. I am also thrilled to work with Akiva again. We have shared some incredibly meaningful creative experiences, and this feels like the right story to bring us back together." As a PhD graduate of Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute and a future king of the techno-thriller, Wilson was the ideal writer to bring this frightening story to life, and a 2014 sequel titled "Robogenesis" was equally gripping. The prolific, award-winning writer has since set up a multitude of other Hollywood projects spawned from his catalog of works, including "Amped," "The Clockwork Dynasty," the authorized sequel to Michael Crichton's "The Andromeda Strain," " The Andromeda Evolution ," and his 2025 alien invasion novel "Hole in the Sky," still alive at Netflix. Daniel H. Wilson's "Robopocalypse" is headed for the small screen! (Image credit: Daniel H. Wilson) Howard's Imagine Entertainment will partner with Akiva Goldsman's Weed Road Pictures on this episodic adaptation, with Howard attached to direct the pilot episode and Goldsman serving as series showrunner. "Robopocalypse" marks a creative reunion f

Wilson Vintage "Daniel created a future that feels both startling and increasingly plausible, with characters who must figure out what connects us when the technology we rely on turns against us. I am also thrilled to work with Akiva again. We have shared some incredibly meaningful creative experiences, and this feels like the right story to bring us back together." Daniel H. Wilson's "Robopocalypse" is headed for the small screen! (Image credit: Daniel H. Wilson) Howard's Imagine Entertainment will partner with Akiva Goldsman's Weed Road Pictures on this episodic adaptation, with Howard attached to direct the pilot episode and Goldsman serving as series showrunner. "Robopocalypse" marks a creative reunion for the distinguished creators, following their collaborations on "A Beautiful Mind," "Cinderella Man," "The Da Vinci Code," and "Angels & Demons." Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment is slated to executive produce the ambitious show alongside Imagine's Brian Grazer and Jeb Brody and Weed's Rachel Wizenberg and Greg Lessans. It's too early to tell which streaming service the "Robopocalypse" TV show will be attached to yet. Hopefully the pilot episode wows one of the big names, and we can finally see the "Robopocalypse" adaptation of our dreams. In the meantime, we'd recommend checking out the original book by Daniel H. Wilson. Robopocalypse by Daniel H. Wilson: was $19 now $10.48 Not far into our future, the dazzling technology that runs our world turns against us. Controlled by a childlike—yet massively powerful—artificial intelligence known as Archos, the global network of machines on which our world has grown dependent suddenly becomes an implacable, deadly foe. item.title: Starfish Space loses contact with 1st 'Otter' servicing spacecraft, ending NASA tech-demo mission
item.description: null Starfish Space's first Otter has died, just a month after it reached the final frontier. The Seattle startup announced on Tuesday (Nov. 3) that its Otter 24C satellite suffered a glitch in low Earth orbit (LEO) and is not recoverable. The anomaly killed an ambitious mission in the cradle, as Otter 24C was still in the commissioning phase. Otter 24C launched Oct. 1 on SpaceX 's Transporter-18 mission, a rideshare flight that carried a total of 130 payloads to LEO (including a prototype satellite for Project Suncatcher , Google's planned AI constellation). The Starfish satellite was flying a mission for NASA called Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability, or SSPICY for short. The goal was to "demonstrate technologies necessary for future debris-removal missions as well as for future applications in the servicing and inspection of active spacecraft," according to NASA's SSPICY site . "This advances NASA's in-space manufacturing and assembly (ISAM) goals to ensure a sustainable space operating environment and builds towards a future where objects can be assembled, repaired and maintained in space, significantly expanding possibilities for science and human exploration," the agency added. Starfish Space was a natural partner. The Seattle company plans to become a big player in the nascent field of satellite servicing , using its line of Otter craft to repair, refuel or deorbit other satellites for a variety of customers. Illustration of a Starfish Space Otter satellite rendesvousing with another spacecraft in Earth orbit. (Image credit: Starfish Space) SSPICY marked Otter's spaceflight debut. The mission plan called for the 739-pound (335-kilogram) Otter 24C spacecraft to approach and inspect "up to four inoperable space objects of U.S. origin" over the course of a two-year mission, performing detailed visual inspections. But Otter 24C never got the chance to perform any of these orbital rendezvous. "While working through commissioning steps, Starfish eventually stopped receiving data from Otter 24C," the company said in a Nov. 3 X post . "An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by [California company] Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications," Starfish added. "Starfish, NASA, and Astro Digital have concluded that Otter 24C is not recoverable." The company further said that it's implementing fixes to reduce the chances that the problem will crop up in the future. And it stressed that Otter 24C's death will not be in vain. "The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions, as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit," Starfish said. The Seattle company plans to become a big player in the nascent field of satellite servicing , using its line of Otter craft to repair, refuel or deorbit other satellites for a variety of customers. Illustration of a Starfish Space Otter satellite rendesvousing with another spacecraft in Earth orbit. (Image credit: Starfish Space) SSPICY marked Otter's spaceflight debut. The mission plan called for the 739-pound (335-kilogram) Otter 24C spacecraft to approach and inspect "up to four inoperable space objects of U.S. origin" over the course of a two-year mission, performing detailed visual inspections. But Otter 24C never got the chance to perform any of these orbital rendezvous. "While working through commissioning steps, Starfish eventually stopped receiving data from Otter 24C," the company said in a Nov. 3 X post . "An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by [California company] Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications," Starfish added. "Starfish, NASA, and Astro Digital have concluded that Otter 24C is not recoverable." The company further said that it's implementing fixes to reduce the chances that the problem will crop up in the future. And it stressed that Otter 24C's death will not be in vain. "The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions, as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit," Starfish said. Otter Pup 2 is now operating as close as 25 meters away from @GilmourSpace's ElaraSat, fully autonomously. This vid contains imagery captured when we were separated by just 33.6 meters.We’ve demonstrated our ability to safely and precisely operate at very close range, executing intricate maneuvers, gathering detailed imagery, and testing the capabilities we’ll need for docking.With this progress, Otter Pup 2 has officially completed Characterize, the penultimate phase of its mission. That leaves just one phase left: attempting docking, and a chance to make history. October 27, 2026 The Seattle company has other work to do in LEO at the moment as well: Its Otter Pup 2 prototype craft is currently gearing up to conduct a historic docking of its own in LEO. Otter Pup 2, which launched in June 2025, has been getting closer and closer to another private spacecraft, Gilmour Space's ElaraSat. Last week, the company announced that Otter Pup 2 got within a mere 82 feet (25 meters) of its target. "With this progress, Otter Pup 2 has officially completed Characterize, the penultimate phase of its mission. That leaves just one phase left: attempting docking, and a chance to make history," Starfish Space said in an Oct. 27 X post . Two private satellites have docked before, but only much higher above Earth, in geostationary orbit . Such a meetup has not yet happened in LEO.

item.title: Revealed: Palantir lobbied minister to stretch AI tools’ reach to NHS GP records
item.description: Exclusive: WhatsApp messages show firm pressuring Zubir Ahmed MP to help bring sensitive data into its platform Palantir lobbied a health minister to consider extending its AI technology into GP records, stretching its reach into the NHS in a way doctors fear could undermine trust with patients. The US company, co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel, used a direct WhatsApp channel to argue that “the logic of joining up primary and secondary [care] data is unarguable” and said its software was “ideal” for the job. The push came in February this year despite GP data being expressly ruled out of the scope of Palantir’s existing £330m contract with NHS England to run its federated data platform (FDP), which it says has helped cut surgery waiting times and discharge delays. The US company, co-founded by the Trump-supporting billionaire Peter Thiel, used a direct WhatsApp channel to argue that “the logic of joining up primary and secondary [care] data is unarguable” and said its software was “ideal” for the job. The push came in February this year despite GP data being expressly ruled out of the scope of Palantir’s existing £330m contract with NHS England to run its federated data platform (FDP), which it says has helped cut surgery waiting times and discharge delays. item.title: Nkanyeziyethu Malunga: The Zimbabwean Designer Preserving African Heritage Through Fashion
item.description: At her workshop in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe, Nkanyeziyethu Malunga crafted colour into fabric, using plants, tree bark and other natural materials gathered from the environment. Choosing a colour or designing a pattern is only one of the processes. Each material carries details on how it was gathered, prepared, and transformed, which Malunga is incorporating into contemporary fashion. “My dyes are mainly extracted from plants such as mnyii and hibiscus. Although I also use many other plants, including tubers, that have properties suitable for dye extraction. I love hibiscus not only for its petals, which produce beautiful dyes, but also for its tea.” The 37-year-old designer is challenging conventional notions about what defines a fashion collection and where creative knowledge originates. Through her clothing business, GANU, she transforms indigenous materials and skills into clothes and accessories, demonstrating how knowledge passed down through generations can inform modern design, provide opportunities for rural women, and conserve cultural practices. Her method is based on teachings learned from her late maternal grandmother, Ngatsha Nkatha, who resided in Tsholotsho, a rural district in Zimbabwe. During the school vacations, Malunga and her siblings traveled from Bulawayo to visit grandma, witnessing as she turned sisal, sedge, and reeds into winnowing baskets. “When I was a child, I often visited my grandmother in the village with my siblings. She was very dexterous with her fingers, and that passion eventually became mutual.” Malunga started experimenting with fashion in her teens before launching Ganu in 2013. The name is derived from iganu, the Ndebele term for marula fruit, and represents her connection to local resources and African identity. Her creations blend basketry, crocheting, batik, and beadwork with natural dyes, leather, and other locally produced materials. For Malunga, the importance of these materials goes beyond their appearance. Bamboo, sisal, reeds, and sedge are used in basketry, and she breeds Angora goats for their fur, which she straightens and dyes to make garments. Cowhide obtained from local abattoirs is softened in a tannery before being mixed into leather designs. “I keep Angora goats for the fur needed in garment production. However, for raw materials such as cowhide, I usually source these from local abattoirs while sisal and tree barks are either harvested by me or sometimes extracted by colleagues I work with, who are based in the rural areas.” Desmond Ntini , a cultural entrepreneur based in Bulawayo, sees Malunga’s work as part of a broader shift in how African history is perceived and used. ” Malunga is redefining the fashion industry by blending traditional African influences with contemporary creativity. Her work explains how our cultural identity can inspire modern designs while opening doors for sustainable fashion, business opportunities, and the celebration of African heritage.” Ntini said. item.content:encoded: At her workshop in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe, Nkanyeziyethu Malunga crafted colour into fabric, using plants, tree bark and other natural materials gathered from the environment. Choosing a colour or designing a pattern is only one of the processes. Each material carries details on how it was gathered, prepared, and transformed, which Malunga is incorporating into contemporary fashion. “My dyes are mainly extracted from plants such as mnyii and hibiscus. Although I also use many other plants, including tubers, that have properties suitable for dye extraction. I love hibiscus not only for its petals, which produce beautiful dyes, but also for its tea.” The 37-year-old designer is challenging conventional notions about what defines a fashion collection and where creative knowledge originates. Through her clothing business, GANU, she transforms indigenous materials and skills into clothes and accessories, demonstrating how knowledge passed down through generations can inform modern design, provide opportunities for rural women, and conserve cultural practices. Her method is based on teachings learned from her late maternal grandmother, Ngatsha Nkatha, who resided in Tsholotsho, a rural district in Zimbabwe. During the school vacations, Malunga and her siblings traveled from Bulawayo to visit grandma, witnessing as she turned sisal, sedge, and reeds into winnowing baskets. “When I was a child, I often visited my grandmother in the village with my siblings. She was very dexterous with her fingers, and that passion eventually became mutual.” Malunga started experimenting with fashion in her teens before launching Ganu in 2013. The name is derived from iganu, the Ndebele term for marula fruit, and represents her connection to local resources and African identity. Her creations blend basketry, crocheting, batik, and beadwork with natural dyes, leather, and other locally produced materials. For Malunga, the importance of these materials goes beyond their appearance. Bamboo, sisal, reeds, and sedge are used in basketry, and she breeds Angora goats for their fur, which she straightens and dyes to make garments. Cowhide obtained from local abattoirs is softened in a tannery before being mixed into leather designs. “I keep Angora goats for the fur needed in garment production. However, for raw materials such as cowhide, I usually source these from local abattoirs while sisal and tree barks are either harvested by me or sometimes extracted by colleagues I work with, who are based in the rural areas.” Desmond Ntini , a cultural entrepreneur based in Bulawayo, sees Malunga’s work as part of a broader shift in how African history is perceived and used. ” Malunga is redefining the fashion industry by blending traditional African influences with contemporary creativity. Her work explains how our cultural identity can inspire modern designs while opening doors for sustainable fashion, business opportunities, and the celebration of African heritage.” Ntini said. Her ventures also go beyond her own label. In 2024, she founded Matobo Goes Fashion And Beyond, working with Matobo women in partnership with Ekhaya-gaia, my beautiful home in Zimbabwe, and the Amagugu International Heritage Centre. The concept transforms traditional hut paintings into contemporary clothes. The project addresses the issue of cultural preservation. Rain can remove paintings from traditional dwellings, putting communities at risk of losing patterns that are not often documented. Reproducing these designs on fabric provides another way to record and disseminate them, as well as introduce the patterns to audiences outside of the communities where they originated. The initiative also provides opportunities for women to share their knowledge and engage in the interpretation of their cultural legacy. Rather than interpreting traditional decoration as something that solely belongs in rural dwellings, the concept incorporates it into a new context while maintaining its connection to the communities that created it. This approach opens up the possibility of adding value to Zimbabwe’s resources and abilities rather than regarding them as apart from the official fashion sector. Zimbabwe’s cultural and creative industries contributed an estimated US$2.7 billion to the country’s economy in 2024, equivalent to 5.92% of gross domestic product, according to a study whose findings were reported in June 2026. The sector accounted for an estimated 22,223 jobs. Dr. Florence Sebele , a senior lecturer and acting chair of the Department of Art, Design, and Technology Education at the National University of Science and Technology in Bulawayo, studies indigenous knowledge in textile technology. She sees Malunga’s method as an opportunity to challenge assumptions about African creativity. “By taking indigenous knowledge that has long been undervalued and transforming it into modern fashion, Malunga speaks to our identity, culture and heritage as Zimbabweans and also as Africans. Her work is a powerful reminder that we have so much to take pride in, while for the wider world, it challenges the dominant narrative of what fashion is and where innovation comes from, showing that authentic, rooted African knowledge has global relevance.” That dilemma is especially important in an industry where African cultural references can be seen on international runways yet the expertise and people that support them receive little recognition. Malunga’s work begins with techniques and materials rooted in local culture and then adapts them for modern applications. Sebele feels that this work has applications beyond fashion, such as cultural tourism, research, and creative enterprise. Its significance stems from making indigenous knowledge visible, as well as demonstrating how it may be used to inform future research and commercial activities. Malunga’s grandmother died before she could pass on everything she knew, leaving Malunga to seek out other custodians of traditional skills. “My grandmother’s death came early, before I could master everything on the use of indigenous knowledge in creating contemporary fashion. As a result, I have also learned to tap into the wisdom of various elderly women that I have come across since embarking on this journey.” Her creations have been showcased on platforms beyond Zimbabwe, including the Durban Fashion Fair in South Africa in 2016. She was nominated for Outstanding Fashion Designer at the 2018 Bulawayo Arts Awards and has worked with markets in Ghana, Europe, and the United States. She displayed under the ZimTrade pavilion at the Zimbabwe International Trade Fair in April of this year, and the organisation’s SheExports initiative has helped her explore international markets. However, the greater relevance of Malunga’s work rests in what occurs before a garment reaches a buyer. Plant dyes, basketry skills, traditional paintings, and rural women’s expertise all contribute to a creative process that bridges generations and creates new avenues for cultural expression. “…we learn everyday, we learn as we go, and we learn from everyone,”Malunga reflected. Malunga’s challenge is to ensuring that this expertise is retained, that the communities that contribute to it are acknowledged, and that the opportunities it offers extend beyond the runway. item.title: Researchers pwn automakers’ Android apps to remotely unlock cars, honk horns
item.description: Security researchers exploited flaws in Android apps to gain remote access to connected cars from two major automakers, allowing them to start engines, flash headlights, and sound horns. Shubham Shah, co-founder at Assetnote, and researcher Sam Curry worked together on the exploits earlier this year. By tinkering with the cars’ Android apps, they devised exploit paths to issue remote commands to vehicles in Australia and the US . The pair published separate blogs covering different aspects of the research; Shah said the US attack "required a lot more work" because the automaker "spent much more time securing the US, Canadian, and European OpenIDM environments." Both exploit chains centered around weaknesses in the ForgeRock identity platform relied upon by both automakers, the identities of which were kept anonymous by the researchers, who have previously highlighted flaws in the likes of Hyundai , Kia , Subaru , and many others . In the Australian version of the app, the researchers first found a vehicle identification number (VIN) using public licence plate checkers, and used those in queries to internal APIs, which provided personal information and owner email addresses. They also found hardcoded admin credentials for the ForgeRock OpenIDM that were meant for the staging environment but also worked in production. After bypassing the heavy WAF filtering by exploiting path traversal flaws, they were able to invoke the internal admin APIs and take over target accounts using only their email addresses. This let them mint authentication tokens, which they could issue to send arbitrary commands to affected vehicles through the mobile app. Issuing commands on the US version also required bypassing WAF filtering through a path traversal, though with a more involved technique: exploiting path confusion to reach the Apache Felix admin console. The researchers used factory default credentials in Felix’s OSGi Web Console to gain admin privileges. They then used Felix configuration manager to schedule a task that executed an inline Groovy script, giving them shell access to the identity servers. The researchers then queried local admin API endpoints, allowing them to view or modify user account data. From there, they logged into car owners’ accounts, and gained the ability to issue the same commands as demonstrated in the Australian version. According to Curry’s disclosure timeline, he and Shah approached the affected automakers in "early 2026," and the exploits were patched within two hours of receiving the report. Although the automakers wished to remain anonymous, it didn’t take long for some petrolheads to speculate that the partially blurred car in Shah’s demo video was a Toyota, citing the shape of the wing mirror and the unlock sound it made. Onlookers claimed that the two automakers in question were likely Toyota and its luxury brand Lexus. This let them mint authentication tokens, which they could issue to send arbitrary commands to affected vehicles through the mobile app. Issuing commands on the US version also required bypassing WAF filtering through a path traversal, though with a more involved technique: exploiting path confusion to reach the Apache Felix admin console. The researchers used factory default credentials in Felix’s OSGi Web Console to gain admin privileges. Onlookers claimed that the two automakers in question were likely Toyota and its luxury brand Lexus. Asked wether the claims were accurate, a spokesperson for Toyota Motor Corporation neither confirmed nor denied them. Curry said he and Shah chose to uphold the manufacturers’ requests to remain anonymous out of concern for infoseccers’ current workloads. He said: "Obviously, they have asked not to be named, and while normally we would fight to actually include the company names, it's a busy time in the security world and I don't like the idea of them diverting resources because they are worried about something with this disclosure." ®

item.title: Nvidia’s board needs to do some succession planning – sharpish | Nils Pratley
item.description: The chipmaker faces business risks and political scrutiny due to its over-reliance on founder and CEO Jensen Huang Why is Nvidia’s Jensen Huang at the centre of a US-China row? Too big – and too well-connected – to sack? One doesn’t have to be overly cynical to think Jensen Huang, the Nvidia boss, starts with one huge advantage as the chipmaker’s board starts its independent investigation into the alleged honeytrap spy scandal . The world of US big tech is not, to put it mildly, strong on checks and balances on a founder’s power. Huang does not enjoy the supercharged voting rights that are par for the course elsewhere – his shareholding is a plain vanilla 3.6%. On the other hand, Nvidia’s board does not appear to have spent much time worrying about succession planning and “key person risk” or other standard concerns of corporate governance wonks outside the US. Continue reading...

item.title: NASA just launched a $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge to award cash prizes to students that solve lunar base problems
item.description: null CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA has officially launched the Moon Base Student Challenge, asking students to help build humanity's future on the moon. And there's $1 million in prizes up for grabs for the winners. To build and sustain a base on the moon , NASA will have to solve a myriad of problems. And they're looking to the next generation for help, the space agency's chief Jared Isaacman said Sunday (Nov. 8). "We are inviting students from across the country to help solve some of the problems that stand between humanity and a permanent presence on another world," Isaacman said. "We're putting 1 million in prizes together to support the best ideas and recognize the teams behind them." Isaacman made this announcement wearing his blue flight suit from the rocket garden at NASA's Kennedy Space Center Visitor Center amidst the agency's MAX POWER air show event . Just the day before, he flew fighter jets in that suit and even jumped out of a plane, skydiving into the event. Soon after this announcement, he was flying another fighter plane above the crowd. The audience for this announcement was filled with students of all ages. Some young children wearing costume spacesuits squeezed as close as they could to the front of the room while teenagers considering their futures listened intently. It was clear that Isaacman's presence and words were landing with this group. But what moon base challenges does NASA want to see these students tackle? In short, all of them. "The moon base will allow us to conduct groundbreaking science, test new technologies, and prepare again for where we inevitably go next, which is the red planet," he said. "But before any of that can happen, we have an awful lot of problems that need to be solved." "We need ways to generate power through the long lunar night . We need to protect our astronauts from that incredibly harsh and dangerous and demanding environment on the surface. We need to move people and equipment around on the surface and support human life three days away from Earth," Isaacman said, illustrating just a few of the big issues that present with the concept of a moon base. NASA Adminisrator Jared Isaacman invites students to help NASA build a moon base at NASA's Kennedy Space Center Visitor Center. (Image credit: Chelsea Gohd) How will it work? This challenge is open to high school and post-secondary students based in the U.S. For participating students, they will form teams that will work on an idea from one of six different technical topics related to creating and running a moon base. These six topics include power systems, habitats, communications, mobility, life support and astronaut safety . This will be what Isaacman described as a "multi-phase competition that mirrors how ideas are developed actually in the aerospace industry." "Teams will first submit concepts, then they're going to refine them, and finalists will have the opportunity to present their solutions directly to NASA leaders and stakeholders,"

"We are inviting students from across the country to help solve some of the problems that stand between humanity and a permanent presence on another world," Isaacman said. "We're putting 1 million in prizes together to support the best ideas and recognize the teams behind them." Isaacman made this announcement wearing his blue flight suit from the rocket garden at NASA's Kennedy Space Center Visitor Center amidst the agency's MAX POWER air show event . Just the day before, he flew fighter jets in that suit and even jumped out of a plane, skydiving into the event. Soon after this announcement, he was flying another fighter plane above the crowd. The audience for this announcement was filled with students of all ages. Some young children wearing costume spacesuits squeezed as close as they could to the front of the room while teenagers considering their futures listened intently. It was clear that Isaacman's presence and words were landing with this group. But what moon base challenges does NASA want to see these students tackle? In short, all of them. "The moon base will allow us to conduct groundbreaking science, test new technologies, and prepare again for where we inevitably go next, which is the red planet," he said. "But before any of that can happen, we have an awful lot of problems that need to be solved." "We need ways to generate power through the long lunar night . We need to protect our astronauts from that incredibly harsh and dangerous and demanding environment on the surface. We need to move people and equipment around on the surface and support human life three days away from Earth," Isaacman said, illustrating just a few of the big issues that present with the concept of a moon base. NASA Adminisrator Jared Isaacman invites students to help NASA build a moon base at NASA's Kennedy Space Center Visitor Center. (Image credit: Chelsea Gohd) How will it work? This challenge is open to high school and post-secondary students based in the U.S. For participating students, they will form teams that will work on an idea from one of six different technical topics related to creating and running a moon base. These six topics include power systems, habitats, communications, mobility, life support and astronaut safety . This will be what Isaacman described as a "multi-phase competition that mirrors how ideas are developed actually in the aerospace industry." "Teams will first submit concepts, then they're going to refine them, and finalists will have the opportunity to present their solutions directly to NASA leaders and stakeholders," he further explained. "The prize money is great for sure, but the the real opportunity is to work on problems NASA is actively trying to solve right now, so students don't need to wait to graduation to contribute to that effort," Isaacman added. A long road ahead Right now, NASA has a long road ahead of them before a moon base is actually built. In mid-2027, the agency is planning to launch its Artemis III mission which will see a crew of four astronauts practice rendezvous maneuvers with two different lunar landers. If all goes to plan, this will be followed by Artemis IV landing humans on the moon's surface for the first time since the final Apollo mission in 1972. The agency is making these big steps forward to not just a crewed return to the moon, but a sustained, long-term return to the moon. However, knowing that a fully-fledged moon base is still firmly in the future, they are banking on the ingenuity, creativity and passion of If you're a student or know a student interested in participating in this challenge, you can find more information on NASA's website here . Interested students can register until Jan. 25, 2027.

item.title: Insight about how 'nature makes no leaps' promises better robot predictions
item.description: Machine learning researchers have developed a technique that allows world models to make better predictions about how objects will behave. World models are used to train physical AI systems like robots how to navigate the real world. They predict the consequences of actions. But they do so based on observed data. These models could provide better direction to robots if they were able to make inferences about possible actions without being trained for all the possible outcomes. Randall Balestriero (Brown University, AMI Labs), Kerda Varaku, and Turing Award winner Yann LeCun (NYU, AMI Labs) describe an approach that might allow that to happen in a pre-print paper, "Counterfactual World Models: Natura Non Facit Saltus." The Latin refers to Gottfried Leibniz's axiom " nature makes no leaps ," which had a good run until it ran headlong into quantum mechanics. Yet for the authors, the saying explains how they have been able to devise a method for zero-shot physics inference. Counterfactual world models, said Balestriero in an email to The Register use "the mismatch between your prediction and the real world to figure out what did you get wrong, and from that you can better understand what happened for better future predictions, debugging, reasoning, all at test time." Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture ( JEPA ) models, developed by LeCun and colleagues back in 2023, have been proposed for robots because they can take an action as input and ask what the world would be like with that action. But a JEPA world model produces an average of outcomes and would not be able to anticipate counterfactual scenarios – events that didn't happen. The technique that the researchers developed is not specific to JEPAs – it can be applied to any world model that predicts the average next state under any action. But JEPA models are particularly well suited to being adapted. Balestriero said that the counterfactual world model experiments were done using off-the-shelf encoders (DINOv2 and MAE) without any fine-tuning and only a small predictor trained on top. Creating a counterfactual world model from that starting point would only require minor additions. Counterfactual world models predict alternative scenarios more effectively by inferring possibilities from what did occur. "In causal inference, answering 'What would have happened had I acted differently?' takes three steps," explained Balestriero. "You use what you observed to learn something about those hidden factors, you change the action, and you predict again with the hidden factors kept exactly as they were. "Our counterfactual world model does all three steps with one subtraction." Balestriero cited an example from the paper: a boat crossing a river with a hidden current and how the JEPA world model and counterfactual world model predicted the boat's movements. "The world model predicted where the boat would end up after steering left, and it actually ended up two meters further downstream," he explained.
